questions.q: Under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, a "contract of indemnity" involves how many parties?
o: Only one party
Two parties — the indemnifier and the indemnified
Three parties, same as a guarantee
Four parties
questions.src: A contract of indemnity involves two parties: the indemnifier (who promises to compensate) and the indemnified/indemnity-holder (who is protected).

questions.q: Under Section 126, a "contract of guarantee" involves which three parties?
o: Only the debtor and creditor
The Principal Debtor, the Surety, and the Creditor
Two indemnifiers and one indemnified party
The bailor, bailee, and a third-party witness
questions.src: A guarantee is a tripartite arrangement: Principal Debtor (whose default is guaranteed), Surety (who guarantees), and Creditor (to whom the guarantee is given).

questions.q: Under Section 128, a surety's liability is generally:
o: Limited to half the principal debtor's liability
Co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless the contract provides otherwise
Always less than the principal debtor's liability
Non-existent unless the creditor first sues the principal debtor
questions.src: Section 128 establishes co-extensive liability — the surety is liable to the same extent as the principal debtor.

questions.q: If a creditor, without the surety's consent, obtains additional security from the principal debtor and later gives it up, the surety is generally:
o: Automatically discharged from all liability
NOT discharged, since this differs from giving up the ORIGINAL security bargained for
Entitled to double compensation
Immediately substituted as the new principal debtor
questions.src: Giving up merely ADDITIONAL security (beyond the original arrangement) generally does not discharge the surety, unlike giving up original security or varying the original contract terms without consent.

questions.q: Under Section 148, "bailment" involves the delivery of:
o: Only immovable property
Movable goods, for a purpose, to be returned/disposed of as directed once the purpose is accomplished
Only money
Ownership of property permanently
questions.src: Bailment applies specifically to movable goods, involving a temporary transfer of possession (not ownership) for a specific purpose.

questions.q: A bailee's "Particular Lien" under Section 170 allows retention of:
o: Any goods of the bailor for any debt owed
The SPECIFIC goods improved through the bailee's skill/labour, until charges for THAT work are paid
Goods belonging to a third party
Only goods worth more than a specified amount
questions.src: Particular lien is limited to the specific goods on which the bailee expended skill/labour, for charges relating to that particular work.

questions.q: A "General Lien" under Section 171 is available to which specific classes of bailees?
o: All bailees without exception
Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys, and policy brokers
Only government bodies
Only bailees who have a written contract
questions.src: General lien (retention of ANY goods for the general balance of account) is limited by statute to these specific professional classes of bailees.

questions.q: Under Section 172, a "pledge" is best described as:
o: A sale of goods with a right of repurchase
A bailment of goods as security for the payment of a debt or performance of a promise
A gift of goods with no strings attached
A lease of immovable property
questions.src: Pledge is a special kind of bailment where goods secure a debt/promise, with the bailor called pawnor and bailee called pawnee.

questions.q: In Lallan Prasad v. Rahmat Ali (1967), the Supreme Court held that a pawnee who retains pledged goods:
o: Can always sue for the full debt AND keep the goods without any accounting
Cannot obtain a full money decree for the debt without properly accounting for the retained goods' value
Must always return the goods immediately regardless of default
Has no rights whatsoever if the pawnor defaults
questions.src: The Court prevented "double recovery" — a pawnee cannot both sue for the full debt and retain the pledged goods without proper accounting.

questions.q: Under Section 182, an "agent" is a person employed to:
o: Only perform manual labour for the principal
Do any act for another, or represent another in dealings with third persons
Only sign documents on behalf of another
Act exclusively in criminal matters
questions.src: Section 182 broadly defines an agent as someone who acts for or represents a principal in dealings with third parties.

questions.q: The maxim "delegatus non potest delegare" means that, as a general rule:
o: An agent may always freely delegate their authority to anyone
An agent CANNOT delegate their authority to a sub-agent, subject to specific exceptions
Only the principal can ever delegate authority
Delegation is always void regardless of consent
questions.src: This maxim establishes the general rule against sub-delegation by an agent, subject to recognised exceptions (necessity, trade custom, principal's consent).

questions.q: Agency arising "by necessity" typically occurs when:
o: The principal has given express written authority in advance
A person must act on another's behalf in an emergency to prevent loss, without prior authorisation
Two parties sign a formal agency agreement
A court specifically appoints an agent for routine matters
questions.src: Agency by necessity arises in emergency situations requiring urgent action to protect the principal's interests, without the usual prior express/implied authorisation.

questions.q: Under the Indian Partnership Act 1932, the defining test that distinguishes a genuine partnership from mere co-ownership is:
o: The number of people involved
Mutual agency — each partner acts as an agent for the others in conducting the business
Whether the business is profitable
Whether the business has a written constitution
questions.src: Mutual agency (each partner acting as agent for the others) is the defining, distinguishing feature of a genuine partnership.

questions.q: Under Section 69 of the Partnership Act, an UNREGISTERED partnership firm generally:
o: Can freely sue third parties to enforce contractual rights
CANNOT bring a suit to enforce a contractual right against a third party, though third parties CAN sue the firm
Cannot be sued by anyone
Automatically becomes void after one year
questions.src: Section 69 creates an asymmetric disability — an unregistered firm cannot sue to enforce contract rights, but remains liable to being sued by others.

questions.q: Under Section 30 of the Partnership Act, a minor:
o: Can be a full partner with unlimited personal liability
Cannot be a full partner, but may be admitted to the BENEFITS of an existing partnership with all partners' consent
Can never have any connection to a partnership
Automatically becomes a full partner upon turning 16
questions.src: A minor cannot contract and thus cannot be a full partner, but may share in profits as a beneficiary with the consent of all existing partners, without bearing personal liability for losses beyond their share.

questions.q: A "Partner by Estoppel/Holding Out" (Section 28, Partnership Act) refers to a person who:
o: Is always a genuine, registered partner
Represents themselves (or knowingly allows representation) as a partner, becoming liable to those who relied on that representation
Has no legal liability whatsoever regardless of representations made
Must always be a family member of an actual partner
questions.src: A person held out as a partner becomes liable to third parties who extended credit based on that representation, even without being a genuine partner.

questions.q: Under Section 4 of the Sale of Goods Act, the key difference between a "Sale" and an "Agreement to Sell" is:
o: There is no legal difference between the two
In a Sale, property/ownership passes immediately; in an Agreement to Sell, property passes at a future time or upon a condition
A Sale can only involve immovable property
An Agreement to Sell always requires a written contract
questions.src: The timing of property transfer is the defining distinction — immediate in a Sale, deferred in an Agreement to Sell.

questions.q: A "Condition" in a contract of sale, as distinguished from a "Warranty," is a stipulation:
o: Collateral to the main purpose of the contract
Essential to the main purpose of the contract, breach of which allows repudiation AND damages
That can never be breached
Relevant only to immovable property
questions.src: A condition is essential to the contract's main purpose; breach allows the aggrieved party to repudiate the contract and/or claim damages, unlike a warranty (damages only).

questions.q: The doctrine of "Caveat Emptor" ("let the buyer beware") in sale of goods is:
o: An absolute rule with no exceptions whatsoever
A general rule significantly narrowed by statutory implied conditions like fitness for purpose and merchantable quality
A rule that only applies to immovable property
No longer part of Indian law in any form
questions.src: While caveat emptor remains the general starting principle, it is substantially limited by implied conditions (Sections 15-17) protecting buyers against latent defects and unfitness.

questions.q: The maxim "Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet" means:
o: Everyone can give whatever they wish
No one can give (transfer) what they do not themselves have (i.e., a seller generally cannot pass better title than they possess)
Only banks can transfer property
Goods can never be transferred without a written contract
questions.src: This foundational rule of property/sale law limits a seller's ability to pass good title beyond what they themselves lawfully possess, subject to specific statutory exceptions.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised EXCEPTION to Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet?
o: Sale by any random stranger with no connection to the goods
Sale by a Mercantile Agent in possession with the owner's consent, to a bona fide buyer without notice
Sale of stolen goods, regardless of buyer's knowledge
There are no exceptions to this rule under Indian law
questions.src: A mercantile agent in possession with consent can pass good title to a genuinely bona fide purchaser, one of several recognised statutory exceptions.

questions.q: An "Unpaid Seller" under the Sale of Goods Act, even after property has passed to the buyer, generally has which THREE rights?
o: Only the right to sue for damages, nothing else
Lien on the goods (while in possession), Stoppage in Transit (if buyer becomes insolvent), and Resale (in specified circumstances)
Only the right to cancel the entire sale unconditionally
Only the right to seize the buyer's other unrelated property
questions.src: These three rights (Lien, Stoppage in Transit, Resale) form the unpaid seller's statutory remedy package under Sections 45-54.

questions.q: "Stoppage in Transit" as an unpaid seller's right applies specifically when:
o: The goods have already been delivered and accepted by the buyer
The buyer becomes insolvent while the goods are still in transit to them
The seller simply changes their mind about the sale
Only for immovable property transactions
questions.src: Stoppage in transit is triggered specifically by the buyer's insolvency while goods remain in transit, allowing the unpaid seller to resume possession.

questions.q: "Delivery" under the Sale of Goods Act may take which of the following forms?
o: Only actual physical handing over of goods
Actual, symbolic, or constructive delivery
Only delivery by registered post
Delivery must always be witnessed by a magistrate
questions.src: Delivery can be actual (physical), symbolic (e.g., handing over keys/documents of control), or constructive (a change in the legal character of possession).

questions.q: In Shaw & Co. v. Symmons & Sons (1917), involving a bookbinder retaining bound books, the case illustrated the practical operation of:
o: General lien available to all bailees
A bailee's Particular Lien — retention of specific improved goods for charges relating to that specific work
The doctrine of caveat emptor
The Nemo Dat rule
questions.src: This case illustrates a classic particular lien scenario — the bookbinder retaining the specific books they worked on, pending payment for that specific service.
